title: The mobile visit for a B2B SaaS company
metaTitle: The mobile visit for a B2B SaaS company
excerpt: Most buyers will judge the site on a phone. The first screen still has to show the product in use and a way to book a demo. Design that width first.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper. The article is about ordering the phone page around the job, not around a desktop frame.
caption: The phone page needs an order you could sketch by hand. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must the first phone screen include?
faqs.answer: Include a sentence that names the job, a crop of the product that stays legible, and a demo control a thumb can hit. Logo strips and feature grids can wait below or leave. The desktop layout should not push those extras above the product on the phone.

faqs.question: How should a product screenshot work on a phone?
faqs.answer: Crop to the record and the action instead of shrinking a full desktop frame until the type disappears. You can use a different crop of the same true interface. Reserve the image's height so the demo button does not jump when it loads.

faqs.question: How do you review a mobile SaaS page?
faqs.answer: Open the live page on a phone, not only in a narrow browser window. Hide it after about ten seconds and ask what the product does and how to book a demo. Then complete the booking with a thumb and fix anything that irritates you.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company mobile website is where most of these buyers will decide to stay or leave. An operator who already runs software checks the page on a phone between meetings. The first screen still has to show the product in use and a way to book a demo. A layout that only works on a wide monitor has not met the buyer.

Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. Design the narrow screen as the page. Let the wide screen add room. The job, the screen, and the demo are the content. Columns are a luxury you add when the width allows them.

## The phone is the review

Treat the phone as the place the work is approved, not as a later adaptation. The operator is in a hallway, on a train, or at the edge of a desk. The connection is ordinary. The time is short. Nielsen Norman Group's summary of page-visit research still applies. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 seconds decide whether they stay. On a phone those seconds contain fewer elements, so each one has to be the job or the demo.

Open the page on a real device before you debate type in a desktop file. If the sentence wraps into a shape you did not read aloud, rewrite the sentence. If the product image is a sliver, it is not showing the product. If the demo sits under a logo bar and a banner, it is not a first-screen action.

Assume one hand. The important control should sit where a thumb reaches without a stretch, usually in the lower half of the first view, or as a clear text button that stays put. A tiny text link in the top corner is a desktop habit. On a phone it is easy to miss and easy to hit by accident when it sits too close to other links.

Login can remain available. It should not outrank the demo for a visitor who has no account. Give each a clear name. Give the demo the stronger visual weight.

## The first screen on a narrow width

Stack the proof in an order that still reads when there is only one column.

1. A sentence that names the job.
2. The product, cropped so the job is legible at phone width.
3. A way to book a demo, with a label that says so.
4. One line on who it is for, if the sentence did not already say it.

That is the first screen. Everything else can follow. A logo strip, a feature grid, and a newsletter field are how a narrow screen loses the job. They can wait below, or they can leave the site.

The product crop is the hard part. A full desktop screenshot, scaled down, becomes unreadable type. Crop to the record and the action. Retake the capture at a sensible width rather than shrinking a 1440-pixel frame until the status disappears. The phone picture can be a different crop of the same true interface. It should not be a different, imaginary product.

Type size should be comfortable without pinching. If the explanatory sentence only works when the reader zooms, it is too small or too long. Shorten it. The phone rewards sentences you can say in one breath.

## Do not shrink the desktop

A common failure is to design the wide page until it looks finished, then let the columns collapse. The collapse hides the demo under three sections the desktop showed beside each other. The phone visitor meets a headline, then a paragraph, then a logo wall, and the product arrives after the patience is gone.

Build the other way. Lock the phone order. When you widen the page, you may place the product beside the sentence. You may not insert new blocks above the demo that the phone would have to stack first. If a block is above the product on a laptop, ask where it will go on the phone. If the answer is "above the product, pushing it down," the block does not belong above the product.

Navigation follows the same rule. The items that matter are the ones in the phone menu, in the order a thumb will meet them. Hover menus are not a plan. They are a desktop convenience. The jobs in the header should be reachable on the narrow screen without a puzzle.

Review both widths every time you add a section. A section that delights on a wide screen and becomes a long tunnel on a phone is a section you add only if the tunnel is worth the scroll. Often it is not. Cut it on both, so the site stays one argument.

## A demo a thumb can use

The demo control should be a real button with words. "Book a demo." Large enough to tap without tapping the thing beside it. Enough space around it that the product caption is not a second accidental target.

The page it opens has to be usable on the same phone. A scheduler that assumes a wide screen, or a form that asks for ten fields, undoes the button. Ask for the minimum. A name. A work email. The job they want to see. They can talk through the rest on the call. The phone is a poor place to write a procurement essay, and this buyer will not try.

Say what the tap does. "You will pick a time." If the tap starts a chat widget, the label should not say demo. Match the verb to the result. An operator who wanted a calendar and got a bot feels misled, and the feeling sticks to the product.

If you offer a video as well, put it below the first screen. Autoplay with sound is a good way to get the tab closed in a public place. Let them choose the video. Do not let it delay the product image. web.dev's Core Web Vitals guidance treats Largest Contentful Paint, interaction delay, and layout shift as the basic loading experience. A good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds, a good Interaction to Next Paint is within 200 milliseconds, and a good layout shift score stays at or below 0.1. A hero video that shoves the demo downward after load fails the shift. A button that waits on a heavy script fails the interaction. The phone makes both failures obvious.

## The product picture on a small screen

Keep the capture light. A huge image file that exists for a billboard will miss the ten-second judgment on an ordinary connection. Serve a size that fits the phone. The wide screen can take a larger file. The phone should not download the billboard.

Leave the picture a stable height so the demo does not jump when the image arrives. Reserve the space. A layout that moves under the thumb is how people book the wrong thing or book nothing.

Test the crop with the brightness down, the way a phone looks outdoors. If the status only reads on a calibrated monitor, it will not read in the hallway. Increase contrast in the product, not only in the marketing type. The interface is the content.

A second picture lower on the page can show the next step of the job. Do not carousel the two. Swipe carousels hide the second claim and often the demo. Stack them. Stacking is clearer, and clarity is the point of the narrow screen.

## What can wait below the fold

Below the first screen, continue the job. A second step. What is not included. A single proof with a constraint and a decision. The demo again.

Pricing can start here if the shape is simple, or it can be its own page linked with the word pricing. Do not paste a full comparison table of tiny text. On a phone, stack the recommended plan and offer the others after it. The shape should still be visible. A table that requires horizontal scrolling is a desktop table that missed its edit.

The about story waits. The blog waits. The partner logos wait, and they may never earn the page. If a lower section does not help this operator decide to book or to leave with a clear no, it is a candidate to cut. The phone is a strict editor because the scroll has a cost you can feel in your hand.

## How to review the phone page

Sit with the live page on a phone, on the connection you actually have. Do not review a stretched desktop window and call it done. A narrow browser is a hint. A phone is the test.

Run the ten-second test. Hide the page. Ask what the product does and how to book a demo. Then run a slower pass. Tap the demo. See whether you can finish it with a thumb. Tap back. See whether the menu lists jobs in words you would say.

Ask someone who did not design it to do the same in a hallway, not at your monitor. Watch for pinching, for missed taps, and for the moment they say they will look at it later on a computer. "Later on a computer" often means the phone page failed and there will be no later.

When the phone page can book the demo, the next failure is usually the page that opens after they decide to talk. A contact path with ten fields will lose the person the phone just convinced. Read [what the contact path should promise this buyer](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you add another required question.

For a sense of how finished product screens behave when the frame is tight, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The phone visit should feel like the same product, not like a poster of it.
